title: Everything Is Hidden
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching is that reality is already present and accessible, and can be experienced directly through a sense of openness and curiosity. This "suchness" or "thusness" involves letting go of our conceptual understanding and dualistic thinking, and instead embracing the interconnectedness and impermanence of all things. By cultivating this awareness, we can find healing and guidance in the present moment, and approach spiritual growth with patience, humility, and inner practice.

sentences.text: So the way I think about Dharma talks is that the community invites somebody to be the spokesperson for our collective mind.
I appreciate the trust and the invitation.
And I don't think it's particularly just me saying anything.
Somehow everything we do is an emergence of everybody we're in community with and practicing with.
So for this day and a half or whatever, somehow we have this deep little community of six people and a whole lot of birds and worms and who knows what else.
So in that spirit I thought I'd explore a little bit that hidden mountain [unclear: "zendo"], the idea of hiddenness.
The title I thought of for these musings is "Everything's Hidden and Nothing's Hidden."
It's so healing to be here, don't you think?
I appreciate Bob initiating all this.
Our coming helps Bob, too, to actually appreciate the possibilities of being in this place or any place.
I had some stress this week, and it was just really lovely to arrive and feel some of that open up and fall away.
As you might have heard from Bob, and you can hear all about it later if you ask him, this place is called Hidden Mountain because the property is the highest point in the local area.

And Bob has tromped around and somehow very scientifically figured out that water goes off in all directions into different watersheds, like the peak of a mountain that you couldn't really see exactly.
And yet here we are on a mountain.
It doesn't look like a kid's drawing of a mountain, it just looks like land and trees and a meadow, this wonderful yurt tucked away here.
And yet from the water's point of view it's not different from any other mountain really, so: Hidden Mountain.
But to the water it's not hidden at all, it's obvious.
The water can see it and feel it, maybe we can too.
In the Zen tradition we have a great affinity for mountains.
Zen temples in China and Japan all have an ordinary name, like our Red Cedar Dharma Hall, Red Cedar Zen Center.
But they also have a mountain name, even if they're not up on some lofty obvious peak, like you think of a picture of the places Terry was in Nepal and Tibet.
I haven't been there, but I read that Mount Tiantong in China, where Dogen studied, is actually kind of a low hill, and it's more or less in the town too.
So not some lofty snow-covered peak, and yet very much a mountain.
Our zendo in town is halfway up a little mountain, Sehome Hill, which is a wonderful little peak.
I've been up there a couple of times recently, after not going there for a decade maybe, riding my bike up there.
It's a beautiful place, right in the middle of our busy town, full of native plants and rock outcroppings and birds like here.
Very peaceful.
So the wilderness is all around us.

We go off somewhere sometimes to find the wilderness, but it's wonderful to be at Hidden Mountain or on Sehome Hill or anywhere, and actually remember that the wilderness is within us and around us all the time.
It turns out that as many of the cells inside the skin are bacteria as anything else.
So we're wilderness inside too.
One of the texts that we chant, which talks a lot about hiddenness, is called the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi.
It's a teaching poem from Master Dongshan, eighth or ninth century, I forget.
And we just chanted that yesterday morning at the zendo.
One of the practices I really appreciate is morning service.
We chant things and we bow.
I think oftentimes we approach Zen thinking it's a very rational, psychological way to heal and de-stress, which seems to be very true, thank goodness.
But I'm also appreciating more and more lately that Zen, like all of Buddhism, is a very devotional practice.
In the senior students group we've been reading this book by a Buddhist scholar.
He's talking about the story of Buddhism, the roots of Buddhism, and to our various delight and chagrin he goes on quite a bit about merit and mystery and devotion.

The purpose of practice in his telling of the story of Buddhism is not just so that the individual practitioners feel better, but that we're helping to generate a field of goodness that helps everybody, a field of merit.
And maybe "merit" is not the best English word to translate whatever the idea was they were trying to get across, because it sounds to us like a merit badge or something, something to get.
"Good energy" sounds too flaky, but something.
So the chanting of sutras, or the chanting of a list of birds' names in this case, that was great.
It's not just so that we learn some teachings that we can apply in our improvement of ourselves, like little wrenches and screwdrivers.
Actually the reciting and the devoting of our attention to these practices of chanting texts is a way to generate goodness in the world.
And then we explicitly give it away.
We often mention the Buddhas and ancestors when we give it away.
We often mention people who are ill or dying or dead.
Or in our dedication this morning, we mentioned the waters and air and trees and nature.
So I want to insert a little plug for the Saturday morning practice at Red Cedar.
Over the course of four weeks, we chant our way through the whole chant book.

So even if it may not be too many people's core practice ever to get up at five something in the morning on a Saturday morning, you might try it for a month sometime and just work your way through the chant book.
It's really wonderful.
Yesterday morning we chanted Morning Service D, which is the only time we access this text, the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, and I was really appreciating it.
The funny thing about this particular text is I remember one time Norman Fischer, my teacher, mentioning he didn't really like it that much.
That's probably just some offhand comment, and he probably likes it fine, but it's funny how that sticks in your mind.
He was critical of it.
He said it was kind of like Cliff Notes for [unclear: "his end teachers"], but I think it's a great text, and I'm sure he appreciates it more than that.
It's so unfair to our teachers, but one little thing they mention, we remember for 30 years, and they probably don't remember saying it.
Anyway, one of the themes of this text, the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, which is an interesting title, is hiddenness.
It's a song for us to sing about jewels and mirrors and samadhi, which is a certain kind of concentration.
The dictionary says hidden means kept out of sight, concealed.
And we have to realize there is much we can't see.
Probably what we can see is the tiniest little fraction of what can be seen.
And yet we're such visual creatures that we take that tiny little fraction and we inflate it as if it were the whole world.
So maybe there's an inherent kind of problem there, a mismatch anyway.
There's this vast world out there, we think, of many, many, many, many things, and we've projected a world on top of that world, which is based on a tiny fraction of those things.
So are they the same world or not?
It's hard to know.
We want to see everything.
We're passionate about this.
We're not narrow-minded.
We want to learn more.
Listening to the bird song all around us, the mind wants to know, what is all this?
We zoom in on certain sounds, and then we realize we missed others.
Tara and I were both remarking this morning, you can hear the train so far away.
There goes the train.
We're listening to the train and something else happens.
And there's the way the mind wants to put a name to everything: that's a train.
That's a bird.
Oh, it's a robin, even better.
The mind likes a fine-toothed comb.
Is that a song sparrow?
What is that one?
But the minute we start thinking about it, we miss something, too.
So our apparatus of trying to see the hidden causes us to miss more that we could see or hear or feel or know.
So what we are is such a mystery.
And so much of what matters to us, even we have to admit we could never see.
You can't see time.
And we are so desperate to have a better relationship with time.
We're upset by time, often worried by time.
We want to have more time, as if we could possess it.
We can see only maybe the effects of time's unfolding, and that matters to us.
But we can't see time.
We can't see love.
We only experience or see what we assume to be from love or about love, joys and sorrows that stem from love.
We can't see it.
We can't see spirit, whatever that is, but it somehow animates living beings.
After a being dies, we know instantly that something has changed.
There's something that was seen that's no longer seen.
You see an animal being very still, and you can tell instantly, right?
You know if it's an alive animal or a dead animal.
But what is this aliveness that's gone or was here?
Eye contact is so powerful because somehow we feel like we can see something, this aliveness.
Why would that be?
The eye is just another organ of perception, and yet we see into each other's souls.
So this text, the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, teaches us that these hidden things are actually right here all the time.
They're kind of hidden in plain sight.
Somehow just barely out of view, but they're right there.
So I just want to bring up a few lines from this text for consideration.
The original text is actually written in couplets in Chinese, but it's hard to translate that into a way that looks like couplets in English.
I've seen attempts and they're kind of stodgy.
So in our chant book, it's just paragraphs broken more or less arbitrarily.
It opens this way:
*The teaching of thusness has been intimately communicated by Buddhas and ancestors.
Now you have it, so keep it well.*
So the opening lines of this poem tell us that whatever this is we're hoping to see or touch, we already got.
It's already been given to us.
It's already been communicated to us by the Buddhas and ancestors.
So take good care of it.
This is characteristic of our school.
This is also Dogen's orientation.
You think you don't have it, but you do.
So the teaching of thusness, thusness or suchness, is a translation of this mysterious word tatata, like Tathagata, one of the names of the Buddha.
It's hard to explain.

It seems to be, in my current sense, a deep appreciation for things as they are, a felt sense of the is-ness of everything, an appreciation of the mountain-ness of a mountain, the sky-ness of the sky.
And it's not rigid or fixed.
It's an appreciation really somehow rooted in emptiness, the emptiness of each of these apparently separate things.
We appreciate the mountain-ness of the mountain when we really feel that it includes the sky and the sky includes the mountain.
Suchness, thusness, tatata.

It's a felt sense of the interpenetration and the interbeing and the temporariness and the fluidity of everything. [unclear: "We go in our backpack in August"], we chant Dogen's meditation on the thusness, the suchness of mountains.
It goes on about the mountains walking and flowing, no different from waters and beings, and that this is of course no less true of us.
But it's an area of our deepest misperception perhaps, that we don't see the thusness of ourselves and others.
But sometimes we do.
We feel it.
Maybe we don't have language for this.
And then when we deeply feel and appreciate suchness, thusness, this sense of things, the poem goes on to say it's really healing.
Suffering and fear melt away.
We're ready for anything.
Because we too are such.
We too are thus.

Appreciating suchness is a kind of letting go: letting go of our illusions of separation and control, of a certain kind of independent existence, as if we didn't depend on everything and everybody every second.
Maybe when I can actually feel the timeness of Tim, I let go of Tim.

And each of us in our own way, opening and merging with each other, and with the birds and the waters and the mountains and the grasses and the pollution and the suffering and the gun violence, everything.
So he says in there, *now you have it, so keep it well.* I think he's actually messing with us a little bit.
There's nothing to have, of course, nothing to keep.
So the rest of the poem he says, well, now you already have it, let me talk to you about how to practice this, how to explore this.
A little bit later he says,
*It's like filling a silver bowl with snow or hiding a heron in the moonlight,*
a heron like the bird.
So snow in a silver bowl, a heron standing stock still in the moonlight, very hard to see.
And yet our practice is to sit still and look anyway.
But what kind of looking?
Not straining to see and figure it out, maybe, but letting the depth of it come forward, come to us.
We step forward and it reveals itself.
Dogen talks about this too.
One moment we can't see the snow or the heron.
The other moment it's so obvious, of course.
There it is.
And time was confusing to us too.
Do we think it was there before and we just didn't see it?
Since we were about three years old, we've believed in an idea called object permanence.
If you don't see it, it doesn't mean it isn't there.
It was there all along.
Little toddlers don't believe that yet, which might have some advantages.
A little later the text says,
*Turning away and touching are both wrong, for it's like a massive fire.
Just to depict it in literary form is to relegate it to defilement.
It's bright just at midnight.
It doesn't appear at dawn.
It acts as a guide for beings.
Its use removes all pains.
Although it's not fabricated, it's not without speech.
It's like facing a jewel mirror.
Form and image behold each other.
You're not it.
It actually is you.*
These texts are so dense.
We chant them and they fly by, which is okay too.
Someone like Dongshan, writing something like this, did he actually intend for us to pick this apart, character by character, or just sort of read it, appreciate it?
I think all these points he's making are about relationship.
Turning away, touching, depicting, seeing, removing.
These are all about relationship: how we relate to the mystery of our life, this life that can't be seen really.
With the usual way of seeing, we can't see our life.
But turning away from that project isn't quite it.
That would be sort of not taking responsibility, hiding out or something.
But trying to grab hold of it is not right either, right?
That doesn't work out.
Turning away and touching are both wrong.
But not turning away and not touching are wrong too.
And trying to depict it in literary form is bad.
So trying to write this stuff down or talk about it, like I'm doing right now, isn't it?
And it's bright when it's dark.
It's dim when it's light.
Somehow it heals us and guides us.
And it's not something we made up, but it's not some unworldly thing without expression either.
"Although it's not fabricated, it's not without speech," he says.
There's an expression of it.
So maybe our life really, in essence, is an expression of something.
And then he throws in the deep mystery of looking at yourself in the mirror.
These everyday things are pretty deep, really.
You look at an image in the mirror, it's not you exactly, but it's not not you, right?
The poet Derek Walcott says that once we've healed from this delusion of separation, you're ready to *peel your own image from the mirror*, he says.
*Peel your own image from the mirror.* He says you can relax and take down the love letters from the bookshelf, the photographs, and the desperate notes.
We need all these depictions of everything.
Once we see it, maybe we don't need all that anymore: our rough attempts to approximate and make sense of things and understand things.
He goes on to say,
*The meaning is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.*
*The meaning is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.* So I think this is a powerful guide pointer for practice.
This way isn't about trying to figure it all out in the usual sense of words and meanings and concepts.
And yet we learn through inquiry, through curiosity, through sitting with our questions and our not knowing.
I started out in zazen counting the breath.
At the time that was the only option apparently available.
You went to the orientation, they said count your breath, and they didn't really talk to you about zazen for a long time.
Eventually, after a long time, I switched to a question.
A teacher asked me to sit with a question.
So I sat for a couple of years with a question: what is it?
That was really helpful.
And he coached me not to be looking for an answer to that question either.
What is it?
Being with curiosity, being with the question, nurturing this inquiring impulse is really helpful, really powerful.
I don't remember any great epiphany exactly where "what is it" broke into a cloud of golden light or anything.
But I remember many moments of just releasing somehow a little bit more into this trusting that reality would reveal itself.
We don't have to look so hard.
What is it?
What is it?
And Dongshan says,
*Whatever this is, is naturally real, yet inconceivable.
It's not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.
With causal conditions, time and season, quiescently, it shines bright.
In its fineness, it fits into spacelessness.
In its greatness, it's beyond location.
A hair's breadth deviation will fail to accord with the proper attunement.*
So the depth of our life that's so often hidden to us is real, naturally real, yet inconceivable, beyond conception, ordinary in a deep sense.
I looked up "ordinary" and it came from the same root as "orderly."
There's a sense of somehow everything is just as it is, in order, ordered by what?
Nature, God, mystery.
But not like a conception of order.
Our conception of order divides things up, puts things in little boxes, but there's a deep sense of order somehow, ordinariness.
In our tradition we talk a lot about ordinary mind, ordinary practice.

And this line at the end of that passage has always interested me: *a hair's breadth deviation will fail to accord with the proper attunement*, which in a way is really encouraging, and in other ways really discouraging.
We're not far off.
We don't need a total makeover, but we're a little out of tune, maybe.
A hair's breadth deviation fails to accord with the proper attunement.
So on the one hand we don't have far to go.
Just a little shift, a little adjustment.
Somehow a natural little settling.
Just moving the dial a little smidge.
It's all the adjustment that's needed to really appreciate our life and the suchness of everything.
We're so close to it, and yet being so close is a huge challenge.
It's just painfully out of reach sometimes, right behind the glass, right on the other side of the mirror.
And so we keep experimenting.
A little tuning here and there.
And of course the minute we turn our attention to this as a manipulation or a way to improve ourselves, we grab hold of that dial, we spin it way past where we need to be.
And we have to start over again.
Slow down.
It's kind of like before a retreat.
If you feel a little resistant, I feel a little resistant, just my schedule and stuff.
Okay, one more thing to do, okay.
Go out to Bob's, okay, okay, okay, okay.
And you get out here and you're like, oh yeah.
Just a little attunement is needed.
How do we do this?
Dongshan brings it back to zazen, towards the end of the text.
He says,
*If you want to conform with the ancient way, please observe the ancients of former times.
When about to fulfill the way of Buddhahood, one gazed at a tree for ten eons.*
So, about to fulfill the way of Buddhahood.
A hair's breadth deviation.
Doesn't mean it's going to be a quick process.
Be ready to gaze at a tree for ten eons.
A few of us have recently been noticing we've crossed the 30-year mark from the beginning of formal practice, and the kind of narrow version of self says, oh, 30 years.
Or, oh darn, 30 years.
What have I accomplished here?
But 30 years is a lot less than ten eons.
Ten eons might be a translation of kalpa.
There are short kalpas and long kalpas.
A short kalpa is the time it takes for a bird with a silk scarf to rub away this enormous granite mountain, which is 100 yojongs by 100 yojongs, an enormous amount.
So even a small eon is a pretty long time.
So we've got to be patient.
But it's easy to be patient, because we already receive this.
It's already been communicated to us.
He says in there,
*When erroneous imaginations cease, the acquiescent mind realizes itself.*
All we have to do is just stop making up the wrong life and the wrong world with our erroneous imagination, our projection out from this tiny sampling that we can see with our ordinary eye.
Dogen also says, you can only see as far as your eye of practice can see.

So now that I've given you this kind of random sample and muddled it up with my attempt to explain, I'll just read the poem, and we'll close with a little more zazen, a little ceremony, and some food together.
And we'll come and go, and the birds will just keep practicing.
*The teaching of thusness has been intimately communicated by Buddhas and ancestors.
Now you have it, so keep it well.
Filling a silver bowl with snow, hiding a heron in the moonlight.
Taken as similar, they're not the same.
When you mix them, you know where they are.
The meaning is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.
Move and you are trapped.
Miss it and you fall into doubt and desolation.
Turning away and touching are both wrong, for it's like a massive fire.
Just to depict it in literary form is to stain it with defilement.
It's bright just at midnight.
It doesn't appear at dawn.
It acts as a guide for beings.
Its use removes all pains.
Although it's not fabricated, it's not without speech.
It's like facing a jewel mirror.
Form and image behold each other.
You are not it.
In truth, it is you.*
*Like a babe in the world, in five aspects complete.
It does not go or come, nor rise, nor stand.* Baba wa wa, that's baby talk in Chinese.
Baba wa wa.
*Is there anything said or not?
Ultimately, it does not apprehend anything, because its speech is not yet correct.
It's like the six lines of the illumination hexagram.
Relative and ultimate interact.
Piled up, they make three.
The complete transformation makes five.
It's like the taste of a five-flavored herb, like a diamond thunderbolt.
Subtly included within the true, inquiry and response come up together.
Communing with the source, travel the pathways, embrace the territory, treasure the road.
Respecting this is fortunate.
Do not neglect it.
Naturally, really, at inconceivable, it is not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.*
*With causal conditions, time and season quiescently, it shines bright.
In its fineness, it fits into spacelessness.
In its greatness, it's utterly beyond location.
A hair's breadth deviation will fail to accord with the proper attunement.
Now there are sudden and gradual in which teachings and approaches arise.
Once basic approaches are distinguished, then there are guiding rules.
But even though the basis is reached and the approach comprehended, true eternity still flows, outwardly still while inwardly moving, like a tethered colt, like a trapped rat.
The ancient sages pitied them and bestowed upon them the teaching.
According to their delusions, they call black as white.
When erroneous imaginations cease, the acquiescent mind realizes itself.
If you want to conform to the ancient way, please observe the sages of ancient times.*
*When about to fulfill the way of Buddhahood, one gazed at a tree for ten eons.

Like a battle-scarred tiger, like a horse with shanks gone gray, because there is the common, there are the jewel pedestals, fine clothing, because there is the startlingly different, there are house cats and cows.
Ye with his archer's skill could hit a target at a hundred paces.
But when arrow points meet head on, what is this to do with the power of skill?
When the wooden man begins to sing, the stone woman gets up dancing.
It's not within the feeling or province of discrimination.
How could it admit of consideration and thought?
Ministers serve their lords, children obey their parents.
Not obeying is not filial.
Not serving is no help.
Practice secretly, working within, like a fool, like an idiot.
Just to continue in this way is called the host within the host.*

A ton more in there. [unclear: "Fought her for many thoughts"], but the other thing about these kinds of texts, too, is we have to have the right conditions, so a little retreat is good conditions, often, for unpacking and exploring these things.
So hopefully this was in some way helpful, or at least generated some good energy in the universe.
This talk and this retreat, our efforts in meditation, if that's what we're doing, may it all bring benefit to us and to everyone we're in contact with.
Thank you.
